title: A century of cholesterol and coronaries: from plaques to genes to statins
funder: The authors' experimental work over 40 years was supported by grants from the NIH (HL-20948), the Perot Foundation, the Moss Heart Foundation and the O'Donnell Foundation.
authorConflicts: Goldstein and Brown are members of the Board of Directors and shareholders of Regeneron Pharmaceuticals.
result: Narrative review. Cholesterol is a 27-carbon, four-ring molecule synthesised from acetate, a two-carbon unit attached to CoA; HMG-CoA reductase catalyses the rate-controlling step. An LDL particle contains about 1500 cholesteryl ester molecules in its core and a coat of about 800 phospholipid molecules, about 500 unesterified cholesterol molecules and one 500-kDa apoB. LDL receptors cluster in coated pits; internalised LDL reaches lysosomes, where cholesteryl esters are hydrolysed. The LDLR gene on the short arm of chromosome 19 has 18 exons and encodes a mature protein of 839 amino acids with seven cysteine-rich LDL-binding repeats and a 50-amino-acid cytoplasmic tail that directs it to coated pits. FH heterozygotes have half the functional receptors and about twofold LDL. Nuclear SREBP-2 activates the LDL receptor gene and the cholesterol biosynthetic genes; statins lower ER cholesterol, activate SREBP-2, raise hepatic LDL receptors and lower plasma LDL. Most LDL is removed by hepatic LDL receptors. PCSK9 binds hepatic LDL receptors and disrupts their recycling. African-Americans heterozygous for PCSK9 nonsense mutations Y142X or C679X had 28% lower LDL and 88% fewer heart attacks. Conclusions on human liver are extrapolated from rats, mice, hamsters and dogs.
